title: Euclid Pre-Registers Dark Energy Benchmarks Weeks Before First Data as DESI Signal Awaits
excerpt: Euclid dark energy benchmark paper published as first data arrives: the Euclid Collaboration’s 114-paper theoretical framework in Astronomy and Astrophysics locks analytical standards before DR-Foundation arrives this month. DESI’s 3-sigma signal for evolving dark energy now awaits Euclid’s
content:
For the past two years, cosmologists have been quietly unsettled. The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) — a ground-based survey in Arizona — has accumulated up to 4.2 sigma worth of evidence that dark energy is not the static cosmological constant Einstein tacked onto his equations, but something that has changed over cosmic history. That is not yet enough to overturn the textbooks. But it is more than enough to make everyone extremely nervous about what comes next.

What comes next, in part, is Euclid.

The European Space Agency's dark universe telescope is weeks away from its first major data delivery, and on Wednesday the Euclid Collaboration published a 114-paper-deep theoretical framework in Astronomy & Astrophysics that amounts to a precise, pre-agreed scoring sheet: here is exactly what Euclid should see, here is what a deviation from expectation would mean, and here is the precision at which any claim about broken physics becomes defensible. Led by cosmologist Noemi Frusciante of the Instituto de Astrofísica e Ciências do Espaço in Lisbon — who trained at the University of Naples Federico II — the review synthesizes years of independent analyses into one authoritative reference paper.

The timing is deliberate. ESA has confirmed that DR-Foundation data lands this month, covering roughly 1,900 square degrees of calibrated images, spectra, and galaxy catalogs. The cosmological analysis the mission was built for will not come until mid-2027, when high-level data products like cosmic shear maps are ready. But by publishing this benchmark paper now, the Collaboration is ensuring the community knows exactly what "success" and "surprise" look like before the numbers arrive.

Why This Moment Is Different From Any Before It

Dark energy is not a new puzzle. The 1998 supernova observations that earned the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011 showed the universe's expansion is accelerating — something that should not happen in a universe governed only by gravity. The simplest explanation, the cosmological constant Λ (Lambda), says empty space has an intrinsic energy density that drives this expansion at a constant rate. That explanation is embedded in the standard cosmological model, known as ΛCDM.

The problem: quantum field theory predicts a vacuum energy roughly 10^120 times larger than the observed value. This discrepancy — called the cosmological constant problem — is one of the most humiliating unsolved problems in physics. If dark energy is not actually a constant, some of that embarrassment goes away. It could instead be a dynamical field called quintessence, or it could mean that gravity itself behaves differently on the largest scales of the universe — not because there is a new substance, but because Einstein's general theory of relativity is incomplete.

DESI's DR2 results this year — combining baryon acoustic oscillation measurements with CMB and supernova data — found evidence for exactly this kind of evolution, at up to roughly 3 to 4 sigma across different dataset combinations. That signal is concentrated in the two parameters of the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) model, which describes dark energy's equation of state as a function that changes over cosmic time: w(z) = w₀ + wₐ·z/(1+z). In this framework, the standard cosmological constant corresponds exactly to w₀ = −1 and wₐ = 0. DESI's data push against those values.

The Euclid review paper is built almost entirely around the CPL model. When the Euclid Collaboration calculated the Figure of Merit — a standard measure of how tightly the two CPL parameters can be pinned down — it found values ranging from 123 to 398 for Euclid operating on its own, reaching up to 1,257 combined when all mission probes are used. Combined with data from the Planck CMB satellite, Euclid is projected to surpass its primary dark energy science goal by a factor of 10 and to improve on current constraints by over a factor of 100. Those numbers mean that if the DESI signal is real and not an artifact, Euclid will almost certainly see it too — and with enough precision to settle whether it reflects new physics or a statistical fluke in the earlier data.

Two Probes, One Question

Euclid pursues dark energy and gravity through two independent instruments operating simultaneously across a third of the entire sky.

The first is weak gravitational lensing, which works by measuring the statistical distortion of background galaxy shapes caused by the mass of everything between those galaxies and Earth. The distortion is not visible to the eye — it amounts to roughly 0.1 to 1 percent of a galaxy's apparent shape, far smaller than the natural variation in galaxy ellipticities, which are typically 3 to 300 times larger. The measurement therefore requires averaging over millions of galaxies to extract the underlying signal. Euclid's space-based position is a critical advantage here: atmospheric blurring — called point-spread function (PSF) systematics — contaminates the alignment signal in ground-based surveys and must be painstakingly modeled around stars in the field. Above the atmosphere, that problem largely disappears.

The second is galaxy clustering via spectroscopy, which uses precise measurements of galaxy redshifts to build a three-dimensional map of how galaxies are distributed in space and moving relative to one another. The pattern of that distribution, particularly its statistical dependence on scale (the matter power spectrum), encodes information about how fast cosmic structures have grown over time. That growth rate is a probe of gravity — if gravity deviates from general relativity on the largest scales, the growth rate changes in predictable ways. Redshift-space distortions, which arise because galaxy velocities add to or subtract from the pure Hubble expansion signal, make the growth rate directly measurable.

Together, these two probes are sensitive to both the expansion history of the universe and the growth history of its structure. That dual sensitivity is what makes Euclid powerful for testing modified gravity: a modification to gravity would affect structure growth in a specific way that cannot be mimicked by a simple change to dark energy alone.

What Euclid Could Measure: The Numbers

The review paper translates these conceptual goals into specific numerical targets.

For the gravity sector, the two phenomenological modified-gravity parameters — μ and Σ, which describe how gravity affects the clustering of matter and the bending of light, respectively — are forecast to be constrained to roughly 24 percent and 3 percent precision. That is an order-of-magnitude improvement over what current data allow. The standard cosmological model predicts μ = Σ = 1; any significant deviation would signal a breakdown of general relativity at cosmological scales.

For the specific f(R) class of modified gravity theories — where the curvature term in Einstein's equations is replaced by a more general function — the Hu-Sawicki model provides the standard benchmark. At a parameter value of |f_R0| = 5×10⁻⁶, Euclid is forecast to reach roughly 1 percent precision, which is sufficient to distinguish this theory from the standard model even at parameter values far too small for any existing survey to probe.

For neutrino physics, the review finds that dark energy constraints remain stable even when analyses marginalize over the sum of neutrino masses and the effective number of neutrino species. In the most conservative case, the sum of neutrino masses can be constrained to less than 220 millielectron volts (meV) at 95 percent confidence — a measurement that would have profound implications for particle physics.

The Warning in the Fine Print

The review's most striking contribution for practicing cosmologists may not be its headline forecast numbers, but a warning embedded in its methodology section.

For spectroscopic galaxy clustering at scales up to k ≤ 0.3 h/Mpc (a standard unit describing spatial frequencies in the matter distribution), one-loop perturbation theory provides an adequate theoretical model. But photometric weak lensing, which probes smaller scales where matter has collapsed into dense, complex structures, is significantly more sensitive to the choice of theoretical prescription.

The paper shows that neglecting relativistic effects — specifically the contribution of lensing magnification to the observed galaxy count signal — could bias measurements of dark energy parameters by 1 to 5 sigma. That means a future Euclid paper that reports, say, a 3-sigma deviation from the cosmological constant could, depending on what theoretical machinery was used, be reporting either a genuine signal or a modeling artifact. For the DESI tension specifically, this matters: if Euclid's future results do or do not confirm DESI, the theoretical choices behind the analysis will be as much a part of the story as the data.

The practical implication is that Euclid's data processing pipeline must include relativistic effects as standard, not optional, components. The Frusciante et al. review is effectively the community's commitment to that standard before the data arrive — a pre-registration of methodology, in the language of open science.

Context: Where Euclid Stands Right Now

Launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida on July 1, 2023, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, Euclid joined the James Webb Space Telescope at the second Lagrange point (L2), approximately 1.5 million kilometers (about 932,000 miles) from Earth, where the gravitational pulls of the Earth and Sun balance.

In March 2025, the Collaboration released its first public dataset — the Quick Release 1 (Q1) — covering 63.1 square degrees of sky, or less than 0.5 percent of the full planned survey area. Accompanied by 27 scientific papers and A&A Q1 special issue published in July 2026, the Q1 release demonstrated the data's quality and allowed research groups worldwide to sharpen their analysis tools in preparation for the larger releases to come.

The first full Data Release (DR1) was originally scheduled for October 2026. ESA announced in June 2026 that it would proceed in stages: DR-Foundation — covering approximately 1,900 square degrees of calibrated images, spectra, and catalogs — arrives this month. The complete release, including the high-level cosmological data products (galaxy catalogs, cosmic shear maps, power spectra) needed for the mission's primary science goals, follows in mid-2027. No official cosmological results will come until that second stage.

After DR1, ESA expects at least four more major data presentations before October 2031, when Euclid's main mission concludes with its third and final full data release.

What the Review Achieves Beyond Its Numbers

The Frusciante et al. paper has a secondary scientific value that is easy to miss in the headline figures.

The Euclid Preparation series of papers was produced over years by dozens of independent research groups using different theoretical codes, different approximation schemes, and different conventions for defining parameters. A Figure of Merit of 300 from one group and a Figure of Merit of 400 from another group are not necessarily inconsistent — they may simply reflect different assumptions about survey systematics, photo-z uncertainties, or nonlinear modeling choices.

The review's core editorial achievement is to unify those analyses — reconciling codes, conventions, and assumptions — into a single reference framework. When the community begins interpreting real data in mid-2027, all groups will be drawing on the same theoretical starting points. That unification is not glamorous, but it is exactly what makes cosmological claims credible: results that depend on undisclosed theoretical choices are not independently testable. The review paper makes the choices explicit and shared.

For Readers Who Want to Follow Along

Euclid's upcoming data releases will be publicly accessible through ESA's science archive. The DR-Foundation release this month will be of immediate interest to research groups but will not contain final cosmological results. The key date to watch is mid-2027, when the high-level data products arrive and the Collaboration begins releasing cosmological papers.

For context: the DESI DR2 tension with ΛCDM, which involves some of the same CPL parameters this Euclid review benchmarks, currently sits at roughly 3 sigma — well-known in the field but short of the 5-sigma threshold conventionally required to claim a discovery. Euclid's projected 100-fold improvement in constraints means that by mid-2027, the community should know whether that tension is real physics or statistical noise.

The scoring sheet is published. The game begins in weeks.

Paper: "Euclid preparation. Review of forecast constraints on dark energy and modified gravity," Euclid Collaboration: N. Frusciante et al. Astronomy & Astrophysics, November 11, 2026. Preprint: preprint on arXiv
